outlook.statement: Plan to grow store count by 13% with focus on new geographies across Central and North India
Formalisation of retail and GST 2.0 rate cut on footwear up to ₹2,500 to 5% are structural tailwinds

The company is entering a deliberate period of capital expenditure with three parts: quadrupling warehousing capacity, owning stores outright when entering new regions (starting with North and Central India), and adding high-quality stores one at a time. The programme will be funded from internal accruals and the Company's own investments, phased over several years, with warehousing capacity sequenced ahead of store openings. Capital employed in the business is expected to rise for the first time in years.
The FY 2026-27 cohort of store openings is already contracted.

The outlook for the footwear and accessories industry remains positive. Growing consumer demand, increasing penetration of organized retail and continued economic growth are expected to support the long-term prospects of the industry. The Company remains focused on strengthening its market presence through customer-centric initiatives, product diversification, operational efficiency and improved shopping experience.

The Company expects demand in the value segment to hold. GST 2.0 has lowered the tax on footwear priced up to ₹2,500 a pair to 5%, the band Sreeleathers has sold in since inception, and the continuing shift of trade from unorganised to organised retail favours a network of the kind we operate. Growth in the year ahead is expected to come from new stores in Central and North India, from deepening the e-commerce channel, and from the warehousing capacity now being added.
The Company does not foresee any liquidity risk.

Market risk: interest rate risk (minimal, no borrowings), foreign currency risk (nil, no foreign exchange transactions), other price risk (from investments in mutual funds and equity instruments at FVTOCI)

Credit risk: from trade receivables, other balances with banks, loans and other receivables; managed via periodic assessment of financial reliability, risk limits, and expected credit loss modelling over 36-month payment profiles

Liquidity risk: from outstanding trade and other payables; managed by forecasting cash flows and maintaining sufficient liquidity; net working capital Rs. 204.27 lakh (FY2026) including cash and cash equivalents Rs. 712.09 lakh
Gratuity plan risks: interest rate risk (fall in rates increases liability), liquidity risk (short-term payout ability), salary escalation risk (assumed 5.50% salary inflation)

Deviation in the rate of increase of salary in future for plan participants from the rate of increase in salary used to determine the present value of obligation will have a bearing on the plan's liability.

Demographic Risk: The Company has used certain mortality and attrition assumptions in valuation of the liability. The Company is exposed to the risk of actual experience turning out to be worse compared to the assumption.

Regulatory Risk: Gratuity benefit is paid in accordance with the requirements of the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972 (as amended from time to time). There is a risk of change in regulations requiring higher gratuity payouts (e.g. increase in the maximum limit on gratuity).
